1.title: Policies and Procedures Across the AI Life Cycle
1.text: Welcome to Module three: Policies and Procedures Across the A I Life Cycle. This is competency C of domain one. You will learn how to create policies that give oversight and accountability at every stage, how to review the policies you already have, and how to manage the risk that comes from third parties.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Create policies for each stage of the A I life cycle. Run an A I inventory and find shadow A I. Evaluate and update existing policies on privacy, security, data governance and intellectual property. Manage third-party risk through policies, assessments and contracts. And cover procurement, supply chain, H R and acceptable use.

1.title: Case Check-In: 47 AI Uses, 9 Unregistered
1.text: At Helios, Mei Tanaka's first A I inventory finds forty-seven A I uses. Nine of them were never registered. That is shadow A I, spread across sales, support and recruiting. At the same time, Ravi Menon is about to sign with Corvid Labs without any A I review. You must write the policies that would have caught both problems.

1.title: Policy, Standard, Procedure: The Governance Stack
1.text: Start with the stack of governance documents. A policy states the rule and its reason, approved by leadership: for example, every A I use case is reviewed before use. A standard sets measurable requirements, such as risk tiers and required tests. A procedure gives the steps, like the intake form and approval route. Records are the evidence that the steps happened. Every policy needs an owner, an approver and a review date. Exam tip: a policy says what, a procedure says how, and records prove it.

1.title: Policies Stage by Stage
1.text: The Body of Knowledge expects a policy topic for each life-cycle stage. At intake: is A I the right tool, and is it allowed? Risk assessment: how risky, and what controls? Ethics and design review: fairness, transparency and oversight designed in. Data sourcing and use: rights, quality and privacy before data are used. Build, test and validation: standards and required tests. Release and live monitoring: gates, thresholds and owners. And records and incident response: documentation, reporting and escalation. Exam tip: name the control that belongs to the stage in the question.

1.title: Intake and Use-Case Assessment
1.text: The first stage is intake. Every use case enters through one door, whether it is built, bought, or switched on inside a tool. Assess the purpose, the data, the affected people and the legal context. Tier the risk so that review is proportionate. Decide: go, no-go, or go with conditions. N I S T expects the mapping work to inform an initial go or no-go decision. Then register the approved use in the inventory. Exam tip: the earliest control is the use-case gate. It stops problems before money and data are spent.

1.title: Risk Management and Ethics by Design
1.text: A risk policy sets a method to identify, rate and treat risks, linked to the organization's risk tolerance. That is Govern one point three. Risk is tiered, with more review for systems that affect rights, safety or access. Ethics by design builds fairness, explainability, privacy and human oversight into requirements instead of bolting them on. Teams document the risks and impacts of what they design and use, Govern four point two, and policies foster a safety-first mindset, Govern four point one. Exam tip: ethics by design means decisions at design time, with a record.

1.title: Data, Development, Training and Testing Policies
1.text: Now data, development, training and testing. Data sourcing rules cover lawful rights, license terms, consent and notice, minimization, quality checks and provenance records. Build standards set approved tools, version control for code, data and models, and secure development. Training rules say which data may train which model, and who approves. Testing requirements cover performance, robustness, security and bias, with pass criteria. N I S T Govern four point three asks for practices that enable testing and incident identification. Exam tip: if data were not cleared for use, no later test fixes that.

1.title: Release, Monitoring, Records and Incidents
1.text: After build, policies cover release, monitoring, records and incidents. Release approval is a gate that checks test results, documentation and sign-off by the accountable owner. Live monitoring needs metrics, thresholds, owners and review frequency, Govern one point five. Records keep model documentation and decision logs for the period the policy sets. Incident response means report, triage, escalate, fix and learn, with a named owner. And retirement means decommissioning safely, Govern one point seven. Exam tip: a policy set with no retirement step is incomplete.

1.title: The AI Inventory and Shadow AI
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. An inventory is a living list of every A I system and use, with its owner, purpose, data and risk tier. N I S T Govern one point six asks for mechanisms to inventory A I systems. Shadow A I is A I used without approval, from free web tools to features switched on inside existing software. You cannot govern, assess or retire what you cannot see. To find it, use surveys, network and expense data, procurement records, and an amnesty to report. At Helios, nine of forty-seven uses were unregistered. Exam tip: the fix is intake plus visibility, not only a ban.

1.title: Reviewing Existing Policies for AI
1.text: You do not start from nothing. The method: list your existing policies, test each against A I risks, record the gaps, then decide whether to update or write a new policy. Privacy policies often miss training use, inferences and automated decisions. Security policies often miss model theft, data poisoning and prompt injection. Data governance policies often miss training-data provenance and dataset documentation. And I P policies often miss rights in training data and outputs, and open-source terms. Exam tip: evaluating a policy means checking it against A I-specific risks.

1.title: Updating Privacy and Security Policies for AI
1.text: For privacy, add purpose and notice for using personal data to train and run models, minimization, handling rights requests for data inside models, and limits on sensitive inferences. For security, add A I-specific threats: data poisoning, model theft and extraction, and prompt injection. Add access control for models and data, testing and red teaming, and supply-chain checks of models and components. Treat model files, prompts and training data as assets to classify and protect. And link the incident process so that A I incidents reach security and privacy. Exam tip: an update extends the old policy.

1.title: Updating Data Governance and IP Policies for AI
1.text: For data governance, add provenance and lineage of training data, quality and representativeness checks, dataset documentation, retention and deletion, and rules on who may use data for A I. For intellectual property, add rights to use data and content for training, ownership and use of outputs, open-source and model licenses, and protection of prompts and confidential data in external tools. Add an acceptable use rule: no confidential or personal data in unapproved tools. Review all of it on a set schedule, and when systems, laws or incidents change. Exam tip: provenance and licenses come first.

2.title: Why Third-Party AI Risk Is Different
2.text: Now third-party risk. Most organizations buy or build on other people's models, data and components. You inherit their data quality, bias, security and legal exposure, and suppliers can change a model without telling you. N I S T names untraceable third-party components and poor supplier vetting as a generative A I risk. Govern six point one asks for policies on A I risks tied to third parties, including infringement of their intellectual property or other rights. Exam tip: buying A I does not buy the risk away. The organization using the system still owns its outcomes.

2.title: Third-Party Due Diligence and Assessments
2.text: Manage third-party risk as a cycle. Identify every third-party A I source, including free tools and embedded features. Tier them by what the system does and the data it touches. Assess with evidence matched to the tier: documentation, test and bias results, data provenance, security and privacy controls, and incident history. Contract the findings into obligations. Monitor and reassess on change or incident, and plan the exit. Exam tip: due diligence is proportionate. Higher-risk uses need more evidence.

2.title: Procurement and Supply Chain Policies
2.text: Procurement is a control point. Route every A I request through the intake gate, so that nothing is bought without review. Keep a list of approved suppliers and tools, with conditions of use. Use the same questionnaire and the same minimum clauses for each bid. Map the supply chain, so that you know which models, data and components sit under the vendor's product. And have contingency plans for failures or incidents in high-risk third-party data or A I systems, Govern six point two. Exam tip: if A I can enter without review, the intake policy fails.

2.title: AI Contract Terms
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Contract terms turn due-diligence findings into obligations. Data use: limits on training on your data, and confidentiality. I P and indemnity: who owns outputs and who covers infringement claims. Transparency and documentation: what the vendor must disclose. Audit rights, incident notice and change notice, so you hear about problems and model changes. Performance and exit: service levels and data return. For high-risk systems, Article twenty-five of the E U A I Act requires a written agreement between provider and supplier. Module twelve goes deeper. Exam tip: a risk found but not contracted is unmanaged.

2.title: HR and Acceptable Use Policies
2.text: People are part of third-party risk too. An acceptable use policy names approved tools, bars confidential or personal data in unapproved ones, requires human review of outputs, and sets disclosure where required. H R policies cover how A I may be used in hiring, monitoring and performance decisions, training duties, and the consequences of misuse. Contractors and partners accept the same rules. Staff need a safe way to raise concerns. At Helios, recruiters use the hiring tool only after training. Exam tip: the quickest leak is an employee pasting data into an unapproved tool.

2.title: Keeping Third-Party Risk Under Control
2.text: Third-party control continues after signature. Reassess on triggers: a new model version, a new use, an incident, or a change in supplier terms. Monitor vendor performance, complaints, incident reports and audit findings. Keep assessments, approvals, contracts and exceptions in one place. Report up: third-party A I risk is a standing item for the A I governance committee. And keep an exit plan to switch suppliers and retrieve data. Exam tip: third-party review is a cycle, not a one-time gate.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Let us recap. The stack is policy, standard, procedure and records, each with an owner and a review date. There is a policy topic for each life-cycle stage, from intake to retirement. List every A I use, and find shadow A I instead of only banning it. Test existing privacy, security, data governance and I P policies for A I gaps, then update them. And manage third parties with tiered due diligence, contract terms, a procurement gate, acceptable use, and ongoing review.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Helios's first inventory finds nine A I uses that nobody had registered. Which policy change best addresses the cause? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Unregistered A I appears when there is no single door for new use cases. An intake gate with tiering and a central inventory makes A I visible. A ban drives use underground, and a survey is too slow.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A company wants its strongest controls in place before any model is built. Which two policies matter most at that stage? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. Before a build, the use case must be assessed and approved, and the data must be cleared for use. Decommissioning, incident response and monitoring belong to later stages.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. An organization has policies for data, development and testing but none for what happens after launch. Which addition best closes the gap in oversight and accountability? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. After launch, accountability rests on monitoring thresholds, a route for escalating incidents, and an owner for each live system.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A company's privacy policy covers customer data collected for service. It now wants to train a model on customer support chats. Which update is most needed? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Training on personal data raises purpose, notice, minimization and rights-request questions that the old policy did not address. It needs A I-specific additions.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A review of an existing security policy for A I should conclude which of the following? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Existing controls still apply, but A I adds threats a generic policy does not name: poisoned training data, theft or extraction of models, and prompt injection. Evaluating the policy means closing those gaps.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Ravi Menon is about to buy an A I tool for Helios. Which due-diligence step best manages third-party A I risk before signing? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Due diligence is proportionate to risk: tier the use, then collect evidence on documentation, testing, data provenance and security. Marketing claims and price-only questions leave the risk unassessed.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. Which two contract terms best manage the risk that a vendor changes its A I model without warning? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and E. Notice of material change tells the buyer the system moved, and documentation and audit rights let the buyer reassess it. The other terms add risk.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: C. Question two: B and D. Question three: A. Question four: D. Question five: B. Question six: C. Question seven: A and E. That completes Module three, and with it domain one. Next, domain two begins with Module four: privacy laws applied to A I.
